title: Starting a New React Project
summary: Create a React 19 project with Vite and TypeScript, learn what every starting file does, and set up git, linting, and environment variables.
intro: React code can't run in a browser as you write it: JSX and TypeScript have to be turned into plain JavaScript first, and someone has to set that up. A template does it in seconds, and nearly every React project starts from one. In this lesson you'll make Trailhead's project in the Playground with Vite, the tool from the web course, and run it. Then you'll learn what every starting file does, how the page boots, the tools that check your code, and the habits every team adds on day one: Git, files it leaves out, and environment variables for settings like the API's address.

steps.title: Making a project with Vite
steps.body:
A React project needs a compiler for JSX and TypeScript, a dev server, a production build, a type checker, and a linter, all set up to work together. Doing that by hand takes hours and is easy to get subtly wrong. A **template**, a ready-made starting project, gives you a setup that thousands of teams already use, in one command.

## Make the project

Open the Playground and its terminal, which starts in your Playground folder, and type:

```bash
npm create vite@latest trailhead -- --template react-ts
```

Piece by piece:

- `npm create vite` downloads and runs **create-vite**, Vite's project starter. `npm create` followed by a name runs the package called `create-` and that name.
- `@latest` asks for its newest version, so you always start from the current template.
- `trailhead` is the name of the folder to make.
- `--` separates npm's own options from the ones it hands to create-vite.
- `--template react-ts` picks the template: React, written in TypeScript.

It asks two questions. **Which linter to use?** Press Enter to keep **Oxlint**, the default, which this lesson explains later. **Install with npm and start now?** Answer **No**, so you can run each step yourself and see what it does. Then it prints the folder it made, and the three commands to run next.

## Install and start

```bash
cd trailhead
npm install
```

`cd trailhead` moves the terminal into the new folder. Recall from the web course that `npm install` reads `package.json`, downloads every package it lists into `node_modules`, and writes down the exact versions in `package-lock.json`. The first example shows what it printed.

Then start the dev server:

```bash
npm run dev
```

The second example shows what it printed. Open the Local address it gives you in a browser. You'll see Vite's starter page: two logos, the words Get started, and a button that says Count is 0. Click it, and it counts.

Now open `src/App.tsx` in the editor, change Get started to Hello, Trailhead, and save. The page changes at once, without reloading, and the count stays where it was. That's the **HMR**, hot module replacement, you met in the web course. For React components it's called **Fast Refresh**: React swaps in the new code for that component and keeps what it was holding. The terminal stays busy while the dev server runs. Press **Ctrl+C** in it when you want to stop the server.

## Pin the Node.js version

Vite 8 needs Node.js 20.19 or newer, or 22.12 or newer. Teams write the version into the project, so every computer that runs it, theirs and the build servers, uses a compatible one. Add an `engines` field to `package.json`:

```json
{
  "engines": {
    "node": ">=22.12"
  }
}
```

npm prints a warning when someone installs with a Node.js that doesn't match. Many teams also add a file called `.nvmrc` holding just a version number, like `24`. **nvm**, the Node Version Manager, is a tool many developers use to keep several versions of Node.js installed, and `nvm use` reads that file and switches to it. Most build services read it too.

## When to start from a framework instead

A Vite project like this one is a client-side rendered app: one HTML shell, with everything built in the browser. React's own documentation suggests starting a new production app with a framework instead, like Next.js or React Router's framework mode, which build in routing, data loading, and the server rendering from the lesson Where HTML Is Made. A plain Vite app is the right start for an app behind a login, for adding React to part of an existing site, and for learning, since you see each piece. This course starts here and adds routing, data, and server rendering one at a time. The Next.js course starts from a framework.

examples.prompt: In the `trailhead` folder, install what `package.json` lists. Your numbers of seconds will differ.
examples.output:
added 28 packages, and audited 29 packages in 2s

9 packages are looking for funding
  run `npm fund` for details

found 0 vulnerabilities
examples.explanation: A new React project needs only 28 packages: React, React DOM, Vite and what it uses, TypeScript, the linter, and a few packages of type descriptions. They all land in `node_modules`. **Audited** means npm checked every installed package against a list of known security problems, and `found 0 vulnerabilities` means none of them is on it. The funding lines say some of the people who wrote these packages accept donations, and `npm fund` lists them. Nothing here needs you to act. When `npm install` reports vulnerabilities in your own projects, the Web Vulnerabilities and Secrets lesson explains what to do.

examples.title: Starting the dev server
examples.prompt: Start Vite's dev server. On this computer another server already had port 5173, so the output shows what Vite does then.
examples.output:
> trailhead@0.0.0 dev
> vite

Port 5173 is in use, trying another one...

  VITE v8.3.8  ready in 333 ms

  ➜  Local:   http://localhost:5174/
  ➜  Network: use --host to expose
examples.explanation: The first two lines are npm saying which script it's running: `dev`, which is the command `vite`. Then Vite found port 5173, its usual port, already taken by another server, so it took the next one, 5174, and said so. On your computer it will most likely say 5173. Recall from the web course that one port belongs to one program at a time. `ready in 333 ms` is how long it took to start. **Local** is the address to open in your browser, and **Network** says the server can't be reached from other devices on your network, because by default it listens on your own computer only. `--host` would change that, which you rarely want.

steps.title: The starting files and folders
steps.body:
A new project has a dozen files, and each one has a job. Knowing them tells you where your own code goes, which files are settings you'll change now and then, and which ones you never touch. ```diagram new-react-project-tree The highlighted files are where the page starts, and where your code starts. ``` ## The page: index.html `index.html` sits at the top of the project, not in `public/`, because it's Vite's starting point: the file it serves for the page, and the file the build starts from. Here it is, as the template writes it: ```html trailhead
``` Two lines matter most: the empty `
`, where React will put the whole app, and the script tag that loads `src/main.tsx` as a module. The next part follows what happens from there. Change the `` here to Trailhead. ## Your code: src Everything in `src/` is your code, and Vite compiles and bundles it. `main.tsx` starts React, and `App.tsx` is the top component, the one every other component sits inside. `index.css` holds styles for the whole page, and `main.tsx` imports it. `App.css` holds the starter page's styles. `src/assets/` holds files your code imports, like a picture: `import logo from "./assets/logo.svg"` gives you its address as a string, to use in an `<img>`. Vite gives the file a fingerprint in its name when you build, so browsers can keep it for as long as they like. ## Files copied as they are: public Files in `public/` skip all of that. They're copied into the build as they are, at the same path, with no fingerprint: `public/favicon.svg` is served at `/favicon.svg`. Use it for files that need a fixed name, like the tab's icon or a `robots.txt` for search engines, and `src/assets/` for everything your code imports. ## Settings - `vite.config.ts` is Vite's settings. Its `plugins` list has one entry, `react()`, which teaches Vite to compile JSX and turns on Fast Refresh. - `tsconfig.json` holds no settings itself. It points to two others, because your code runs in two places. `tsconfig.app.json` is for `src/`, which runs in a browser, so it knows about the DOM. `tsconfig.node.json` is for `vite.config.ts`, which runs in Node.js while Vite starts. - `.oxlintrc.json` turns on the linter's rules, and `.gitignore` lists what Git leaves out. Both come later in this lesson. - `README.md` describes the project, in Markdown, the plain text format with simple marks for headings and lists. ## package.json and the lockfile The example shows `package.json` as the template writes it. Besides the **scripts**, it lists two kinds of packages. **dependencies** are what your app runs in the browser: React and React DOM. **devDependencies** are tools used only while you build: TypeScript, Vite and its React plugin, the linter, and `@types` packages, which describe the types of packages written in plain JavaScript. `package-lock.json` records the exact version of every package that was installed, including the packages those packages need. You never edit it, and you always keep it with the project, so everyone installs exactly the same code. ## Clear out the starter The logos and the counter are Vite's demo. Delete `src/App.css`, the files in `src/assets/`, and `public/icons.svg`. Empty `src/index.css` without deleting it, since `main.tsx` imports it. Then replace `App.tsx` with the start of the shop, in the second example.

examples.title: The template's package.json
examples.prompt: `package.json` in the new project, as create-vite wrote it.
examples.explanation: `"private": true` stops `npm publish` from putting the project on npm by mistake. `"type": "module"` makes `.js` files in it ES modules, so `import` and `export` work everywhere. The four scripts are what you'll run: `npm run dev` starts the dev server, `npm run build` checks the types with `tsc -b` and then builds into `dist/`, `npm run lint` runs the linter, and `npm run preview` serves that build so you can try it. The `^` in `^19.3.1` lets `npm install` pick any newer 19 version, since those promise not to break anything. The `~` in `~7.0.2` allows only newer 7.0 versions, because TypeScript can add new checks even in a version like 7.1.

examples.title: The shop's first App
examples.prompt: `src/App.tsx`, cleared of the demo. Save it with the dev server running and the page changes at once.
examples.explanation: That's a whole component: a function that returns JSX, which the lesson Components, JSX, and Props explained. `export default` makes `App` the file's main export, and `main.tsx` imports it by that name. The page now shows Trailhead as a heading and one line of text, in the browser's plain default styles, since `index.css` is empty. The import of `App.css` and the pictures are gone, so nothing points at the files you deleted. If the page goes blank instead, a missing file is the usual reason, and the browser's console names it.

steps.title: How the page boots
steps.body:
When a React app shows a blank page, the cause is nearly always somewhere in its first second: a script that didn't load, a root element that isn't there, an error in the first render. Knowing the order things happen in tells you where to look. ```diagram new-react-project-boot The left column is npm run dev, and the right is what a build changes. Steps 4 and 5 are the same in both. ``` ## In development Follow the left column of the diagram. **Step 1.** The browser asks for `/`, and Vite sends `index.html`. It adds two scripts of its own to the top first, as the first example shows: one connects to the dev server for HMR, and one sets up Fast Refresh. **Step 2.** The script tag asks for `/src/main.tsx`. Browsers can't run TSX, so Vite compiles it at the moment it's asked for: it removes the types and turns the JSX into function calls, and sends back plain JavaScript. **Step 3.** `main.tsx` imports other files, and each import is another request, compiled the same way: `App.tsx`, `index.css`, and packages like `react`. Recall from the web course that Vite pre-bundles packages from `node_modules` once, so they load as a few files instead of hundreds. **Step 4.** `main.tsx` runs, and React starts. **Step 5.** The browser lays out and paints what React made. ## main.tsx, line by line ```tsx import { StrictMode } from 'react' import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client' import './index.css' import App from './App.tsx' createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render( , ) ``` Importing `./index.css` tells Vite to add those styles to the page. `document.getElementById('root')` finds the empty div from `index.html`. It could return `null` if there were no such element, and `createRoot` won't take `null`, so the `!` after it tells TypeScript you're sure it's there. If you're wrong, for instance after renaming the div in `index.html`, the page stays blank and the console shows Target container is not a DOM element. `createRoot` hands that element to React: from now on, everything inside it belongs to React, and no other code should change it. `.render(...)` gives React the element tree to draw there, and React calls `App`, builds the DOM inside the div, and the browser paints it. An app usually has exactly one root. ## StrictMode `StrictMode` wraps the app in extra checks that run only in development. The one you'll notice: React calls each of your components twice for every render, and uses only one of the results. That's on purpose. A component is supposed to be pure, giving the same JSX for the same props without changing anything outside itself, as the lesson Components, JSX, and Props explained. If calling it twice changes what you see, or does something twice, it isn't pure, and you find out now, not later. The second example shows the double call. So a `console.log` in a component prints twice in development. Leave StrictMode on. In a build it does nothing, and costs nothing. ## After a build The right column of the diagram is a build. `npm run build` compiles everything ahead of time, so the browser never sees a `.tsx` file. Here's the `dist/index.html` it made for the starter project: ```html trailhead
``` The script tag now points at one bundle, with a fingerprint in its name, holding your code and React, already compiled and minified. The CSS has its own file. Steps 2 and 3 collapse into one download, and from step 4 on, everything is the same as in development.

examples.title: The page the dev server sends
examples.prompt: With `npm run dev` running, ask for the page from your computer's own terminal. Use the port your dev server printed.
examples.explanation: It's your `index.html` with two scripts added at the top of the `<head>`. The first imports from `/@react-refresh`, a path Vite serves itself, and gets the page ready for Fast Refresh, so a saved component can be swapped in while it keeps its state. The second loads `/@vite/client`, which opens a connection back to the dev server and listens for changes: when you save a file, the server tells the page what to swap. Neither of them is in a build. The rest is the file you wrote, still with its empty root div, and a script tag asking for `/src/main.tsx`, a TypeScript file the browser will get as compiled JavaScript.

examples.title: StrictMode calls each component twice
examples.prompt: Add a log to `src/App.tsx`, then load the page with the browser's Console open, in the browser's DevTools.
examples.explanation: The page rendered once, and the log printed twice. That's StrictMode calling `App` a second time, to check it gives the same result. Logging is harmless, so this component passes. A component that did something real while rendering, like adding to a list outside itself, would do it twice, and the doubled result on screen would show you the bug. With React DevTools installed, the second line shows in gray, so you can tell which call it came from. After `npm run build`, the same page logs App rendered once.

steps.title: Type checks, linting, and plugins
steps.body:
Vite is fast partly because it checks nothing. It removes the types without reading them, so a type error never stops your page. The tools around it are what catch those mistakes, and this part sets them up, along with the plugins and browser tools the course uses.

## Vite removes types, tsc checks them

Recall from Components, JSX, and Props that TypeScript's types say what each value holds. They only help if something reads them. Vite doesn't: in the first example, a misspelled property shows up on the page as $NaN, and Vite reports nothing.

**tsc** is TypeScript's compiler. In this project it only checks, without writing any files, since the tsconfig files set `noEmit`. Run `npx tsc -b` to check the whole project. The `-b`, for build mode, follows `tsconfig.json`'s references and checks both the app and `vite.config.ts`. It saves what it learned in `node_modules/.tmp`, so the next check is faster. `npm run build` runs `tsc -b` first, so a type error stops a build before it can reach anyone. Editors that understand TypeScript run the same checks as you type, and underline the mistake.

## The linter

A **linter** reads your code for patterns that are probably bugs, even when the code is valid. The template's linter is **Oxlint**, and `npm run lint` runs it. Its settings live in `.oxlintrc.json`. The `plugins` line turns on Oxlint's `react` plugin, and that alone brings React rules that catch likely bugs, as warnings. Three of them matter in the Effects, Refs, and Browser APIs lesson: `exhaustive-deps`, `set-state-in-effect`, and `refs`. The `rules` list then sets two more:

- `rules-of-hooks`, an error, checks that hooks like `useState` are called the way React needs. The State and Events lesson explains those rules.
- `only-export-components`, a warning, checks that a component's file exports only components. Fast Refresh can keep a component's state only when the file holds nothing else, so a helper function belongs in its own file, like `src/lib/format.ts`. The second example shows the warning.

A warning is printed, but `npm run lint` still succeeds. An error makes it fail, and a failing check is what stops a broken change in CI, which the next part explains. So this course makes those three rules errors too. Here's the whole file, with them added as the last three lines of `rules`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "./node_modules/oxlint/configuration_schema.json",
  "plugins": ["react", "typescript", "oxc"],
  "rules": {
    "react/rules-of-hooks": "error",
    "react/only-export-components": ["warn", { "allowConstantExport": true }],
    "react/exhaustive-deps": "error",
    "react/set-state-in-effect": "error",
    "react/refs": "error"
  }
}
```

`npm run build` doesn't run the linter, so run it yourself, or let your editor show its warnings. Many teams use **ESLint** instead, an older and slower linter with more plugins. It was create-vite's other choice.

## Two plugins: Tailwind and the React Compiler

Vite does more through **plugins**, listed in `vite.config.ts`. The course adds two.

**Tailwind**, from the web course, styles Trailhead, with **clsx**, a small function for joining class names, which Components, JSX, and Props uses:

```bash
npm install tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite clsx
```

Then put one line at the top of `src/index.css`:

```css
@import "tailwindcss";
```

The **React Compiler** rewrites your components as they're built, so they skip work when nothing they depend on has changed. The Re-rendering and Performance lesson explains what that saves. It runs inside **Babel**, an older JavaScript compiler, so Vite runs Babel just for it:

```bash
npm install -D babel-plugin-react-compiler @rolldown/plugin-babel @babel/core
```

The `-D` saves them as devDependencies. The third example shows `vite.config.ts` with both plugins. create-vite has a `react-compiler-ts` template that starts with the compiler on, too.

## A shorter way to import

Folders get deep, and imports like `../../lib/format` get hard to read. An **alias** gives `src` a short name: with it, `@/lib/format` means `src/lib/format` from any file. It takes two settings that agree. In `tsconfig.app.json`, inside `compilerOptions`, add `"paths": { "@/*": ["./src/*"] }` so TypeScript understands it, and in `vite.config.ts`, `resolve: { tsconfigPaths: true }` tells Vite to read the same setting. The next two lessons keep relative imports, so each one shows where its file is. From Effects, Refs, and Browser APIs on, the examples use `@/`.

## React DevTools

Install **React Developer Tools** from your browser's extension store: it's there for Chrome, Edge, and Firefox. Until you do, every page you load in development prints a reminder in the console: Download the React DevTools for a better development experience. With it installed, DevTools gets two new tabs. **Components** shows the tree of your components, and clicking one shows its props and state, which you can change right there to see what happens. **Profiler** records which components rendered and how long they took, which the Re-rendering and Performance lesson uses.

examples.title: A mistake only tsc catches
examples.prompt: In `src/App.tsx`, the product's price is misspelled as `pack.price`. With the dev server running, the page shows Trail Pack 45L: $NaN. Check the project in the terminal.
examples.output:
src/App.tsx:12:40 - error TS2339: Property 'price' does not exist on type 'Product'.

12         {pack.name}: {formatPrice(pack.price)}
                                          ~~~~~


Found 1 error in src/App.tsx:12
examples.explanation: `src/App.tsx:12:40` is the file, the line, and the column. `TS2339` is the error's number, which is handy to search for, and the message says what's wrong: a `Product` has no property called `price`. Under it is the line itself, with `~` under the mistake. The field is `priceCents`. Vite ran the same code without a word: the property was `undefined`, `undefined / 100` is `NaN`, short for not a number, and the price formatter printed $NaN. That's the job tsc does that Vite doesn't. The same check is the first half of `npm run build`, so this project wouldn't build until it's fixed.

examples.title: The linter's Fast Refresh warning
examples.prompt: A component file, `src/components/ProductCard.tsx`, that also exports its own `formatPrice` helper. Run the linter.
examples.output:
> trailhead@0.0.0 lint
> oxlint


  ⚠ react(only-export-components): Fast refresh only works when a file only exports components. Use a new file to share constants or functions between components.
   ╭─[src/components/ProductCard.tsx:6:17]
 5 │
 6 │ export function formatPrice(cents: number): string {
   ·                 ───────────
 7 │   return new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" }).format(cents / 100);
   ╰────

Found 1 warning and 0 errors.
Finished in 8ms on 5 files with 116 rules using 14 threads.
examples.explanation: `⚠` marks a warning, and `react(only-export-components)` names the rule. The message explains it: Fast Refresh only works when a file exports nothing but components. With a helper exported too, saving the file makes Vite reload the whole page instead, and everything on it loses its state. The box shows where, line 6, column 17, with a line under `formatPrice`. The fix is the one the message suggests: move `formatPrice` into `src/lib/format.ts`, and import it in the card. The last lines count what it found, in five files, in a few milliseconds.

examples.title: vite.config.ts with the course's plugins
examples.prompt: `vite.config.ts` after installing Tailwind and the React Compiler, with the `@/` alias turned on.
examples.explanation: `defineConfig` changes nothing at run time: it tells your editor what the settings object can hold, so it can suggest names and catch typos. `plugins` run in order. `react()` compiles JSX and turns on Fast Refresh. `babel(...)` runs Babel with `reactCompilerPreset()`, which the React plugin provides, to apply the React Compiler to your components. `tailwindcss()` finds the class names in your files and makes the CSS for them. `resolve.tsconfigPaths` makes Vite read the `paths` setting from `tsconfig.app.json`, which is where `@/` is defined. After any change to this file, Vite restarts the dev server by itself.

steps.title: Git and what it leaves out
steps.body:
Every team keeps its code in Git, and the first commit decides what goes in. A `node_modules` folder committed by mistake makes every copy of the project hundreds of megabytes bigger, forever. A password committed by mistake is leaked, even after you delete it, because Git remembers every version.

## Git in brief

**Git** is a version control system: it records snapshots of your project's files, called **commits**, each with a message saying what changed and why. You can see what changed between any two commits, go back to an earlier one, and work on the same code as other people without overwriting each other's work. A folder Git keeps track of is a **repository**, and sites like GitHub and GitLab keep a copy of a repository online, for a team to share.

Start one in the `trailhead` folder:

```bash
git init -b main
```

`git init` makes the folder a repository and prints where it put Git's own files, a hidden `.git` folder. `-b main` names the first **branch**, the line of commits you're on, `main`, the name most teams use.

## What to leave out

`.gitignore` lists files Git should act as if it can't see, one pattern per line. The template's already covers the important ones:

- `node_modules`: anyone can rebuild it from the lockfile with `npm install`, and it's huge.
- `dist`: `npm run build` makes it again whenever you need it.
- `*.local`: files ending in `.local`, like `.env.local`, which hold settings for your computer alone. The last part of this lesson uses them.
- logs, and the folders some editors make, like `.idea`.

The Testing lessons make folders of reports, so add them now, at the end of `.gitignore`:

```text
# Test output
coverage
playwright-report
test-results
```

The example checks what Git sees after that.

## The first commit

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Start Trailhead from the Vite React template"
```

`git add .` picks every file Git can see, in this folder and below, for the next commit, and `git commit` records them with your message. Git prints the start of the new commit's ID and how many files went in.

## The lockfile, and npm ci

Commit `package-lock.json` with everything else. It's what makes your teammates, and the servers that build your app, install exactly the versions you tested with.

Those servers run **CI**, continuous integration: a service that installs, type checks, lints, tests, and builds the project on every change someone sends to the shared repository, so a broken change is caught before it's merged. In CI, use `npm ci` instead of `npm install`. It deletes `node_modules`, installs exactly what the lockfile says, and stops with an error if `package.json` and the lockfile disagree, where `npm install` would quietly update the lockfile instead.

## A README

The template's `README.md` describes the template. Replace it with what a new teammate needs: what the project is, how to install and start it, which scripts exist, and which environment variables it needs, which the next part explains. A README is the first file people open on GitHub, so a few clear lines there save everyone time.

examples.title: What Git sees, and what it ignores
examples.prompt: In the new repository, with the test folders added to `.gitignore`, a `.env.local` file, a `dist` from a build, and a `coverage` folder from a test run. `--short` prints one line per file, and `--ignored` adds the ignored ones.

?? .oxlintrc.json

examples.explanation: `??` marks an **untracked** file: one Git can see but hasn't recorded yet. These are what `git add .` would pick up for the first commit: the source, the settings, the lockfile, and two environment files the next part explains. `!!` marks an ignored file, which `git add .` skips. `node_modules/` and `dist/` are left out, `coverage/` is left out by the lines you added, and `.env.local` is left out by the template's `*.local` pattern, so your own settings never reach the shared repository. If something you meant to ignore shows up with `??`, fix `.gitignore` before you commit.

steps.title: Environment variables
steps.body:
On your computer, Trailhead talks to an API on your computer. In production, it talks to the real API at another address. Editing the code before every build is a mistake waiting to happen. **Environment variables** let the same code read different settings in different places.

## .env files

An **environment variable** is a named setting that a program gets from outside its code. Vite reads them from `.env` files: plain text, one `NAME=value` per line.

```env
VITE_API_URL=/v1
```

`/v1` is a path on the dev server's own address. In the Routing and App Structure lesson, you'll add the Trailhead API, the course's practice server, to your Playground, in a `trailhead-api` folder next to `trailhead`. From then on, the dev server passes every request under `/v1` on to it, with the proxy you met in the web course.

Vite looks for these files, in the project's top folder:

- `.env`: used every time.
- `.env.local`: used every time, but only on your computer, since `.gitignore` leaves out `*.local`.
- `.env.development` and `.env.production`: used only in that **mode**. `npm run dev` runs in development mode, and `npm run build` in production mode.
- `.env.development.local` and `.env.production.local`: that mode, on your computer only.

When two files set the same name, the more specific file wins: a mode's `.local` file beats the mode's file, which beats `.env.local`, which beats `.env`. A variable that's already set in the terminal when Vite starts beats them all. So with the line above in `.env` and this one in `.env.production`, the dev server uses your computer's API, and a build uses the real one:

```env
VITE_API_URL=https://api.trailhead.example/v1
```

Vite reads the files when it starts. Change one while the dev server runs, and it notices and restarts by itself.

## VITE_ and import.meta.env

Your code reads the values from `import.meta.env`: `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`. Only names that start with `VITE_` get there. Anything else in the files is left out, so if `.env.local` held `PAYMENTS_SECRET=...`, then `import.meta.env.PAYMENTS_SECRET` would be `undefined`. That prefix is a safety catch against sending a server's secrets to the browser by accident.

Vite adds a few of its own, too: `import.meta.env.MODE` is `"development"` or `"production"`, and `DEV` and `PROD` are `true` or `false` to match.

## Typing them

TypeScript doesn't know your variables' names, so a typo like `VITE_API_ULR` would go unnoticed. Describe them in `src/vite-env.d.ts`, as the first example shows. A `.d.ts` file holds only types, and no code that runs.

## Every VITE_ value is public

Here's the catch. Vite doesn't look values up when the page runs: when it builds, it replaces each `import.meta.env.VITE_...` with the value itself, written into the bundle as plain text. Anyone can open DevTools, look at your JavaScript, and read it, as the second example shows.

So a `VITE_` variable can hold an address, a feature switch, or a **publishable key**, one a service gives you to put in a browser. It must never hold a secret: a database password, or a key that can spend money or read other people's data. Secrets stay on a server, and the Web Vulnerabilities and Secrets lesson shows how a browser app uses them without ever seeing them.

## .env.example

`.env` and `.env.production` here hold nothing private, so they go into Git, and the whole team gets the same defaults. Many teams keep every `.env` file out of Git, so nobody can commit a secret by mistake. They commit a `.env.example` instead, listing every variable with a harmless sample value, and a new teammate copies it to `.env.local` and fills it in. Either way, every name your code reads is written down somewhere in the repository, and your README says where.

The project is ready, and its page shows what you wrote and nothing more. The next lesson, State and Events, makes it respond to clicks and typing.

examples.title: Typed environment variables
examples.prompt: `src/vite-env.d.ts`, which tells TypeScript which variables the project expects.
examples.explanation: An **interface** is another way to write a type, and TypeScript merges interfaces that share a name, so these add to the `ImportMetaEnv` that Vite's own types already describe. `readonly` means your code can read the value but not assign to it, and `string` says it's text, since every value in a `.env` file is. With this file in place, `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL` is a `string` everywhere, and your editor suggests the name as you type. Read it in one place, like the API client that the Calling APIs From React lesson writes in `src/lib/api.ts`, so the rest of the app never touches `import.meta.env` itself.

examples.title: The value, written into the bundle
examples.prompt: After `npm run build`, search the built JavaScript for the production API's address. Then count the lines holding the value of `PAYMENTS_SECRET`, which is in `.env.local`, without the prefix.
examples.explanation: `grep` searches files for text, and `-o` prints only the part that matched. The first command found the production address inside the bundle: the build took it from `.env.production` and wrote it in where the code said `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`. The value in `.env` wasn't used, since the build ran in production mode. The second command counts the lines holding the secret's value, and `-c`, for count, printed 0: without the prefix, it never reached the bundle. Anything with `VITE_` in front would have, so read every `VITE_` value as something the whole world can see.

recap:
- npm create vite@latest with the react-ts template makes a project, npm install installs it, and npm run dev serves it with Fast Refresh.
- index.html holds the root div and loads src/main.tsx, App.tsx is the top component, public/ is copied as is, and src/assets/ is for files your code imports.
- main.tsx calls createRoot on the root div and renders App inside StrictMode, which calls each component twice in development only.
- In development Vite compiles each file on request, and a build sends one fingerprinted bundle instead.
- Vite removes types without checking them, so run tsc -b, which npm run build also does, and npm run lint for the linter.
- vite.config.ts lists plugins: react(), Tailwind, and the React Compiler through Babel.
- Commit the lockfile, leave out node_modules, dist, test output, and .local files, and use npm ci in CI.
- Only VITE_ variables reach your code, through import.meta.env, and they're written into the bundle, so they're never secret.
